div.p: Vietnamese social media contains personal accounts of distress, but developing reliable text classifiers requires task-specific annotation and careful separation between emotional expression and clinical diagnosis. This study presents VietDepression, a data construction and benchmarking framework based on 125,329 collected YouTube comments and a final human-labeled subset of 9,134 texts. A weighted lexicon with 335 scoring entries supports candidate selection, while blind annotation and six rounds of active learning address label scarcity. On 343 evaluable human-labeled examples, the weak labeler achieves 0.9787 positiveclass recall and 0.6133 precision, demonstrating its value for retrieval but also the need for contextual review. We compare sparse lexical classifiers, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, PhoBERT, topicbased classification, and a PhoBERT-BERTopic feature combination. On the 1,371-example in-domain test set, the reported macro F1 is 0.7187 for PhoBERT, 0.7153 for the hybrid model, and 0.7138 for TF-IDF with logistic regression. Evaluation on a balanced 3,084-example subset derived from UIT-VSMEC yields a reported PhoBERT macro F1 of 0.3608. This transfer experiment changes both data source and label definition because sadness and fear are used as proxies for distress. The resulting 0.3579 macro-F1 difference therefore measures a combined transfer difficulty rather than a pure domain effect. Classweighting comparisons and qualitative analysis identify class imbalance, contextual ambiguity, and implicit expression as important challenges. The findings support Vietnamese language models as useful in-domain baselines, while emphasizing that annotation validity, evaluation provenance, and aligned external labels are necessary before broader claims of generalization or clinical utility.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Public social media provides a setting in which people describe emotional difficulties in their own words. These descriptions can include exhaustion, loneliness, hopelessness, and loss of interest, but they also include jokes, quotations, encouragement, and discussion of other people. A language model must distinguish these uses if its predictions are to support meaningful research. Earlier studies of mental-health signals on Twitter and online forums established the relevance of computational language analysis to this problem [1], [2], [3]. They also motivate a careful distinction between the unit that is classified and the person whose language produced it. A label attached to a comment does not establish the mental-health status of its author.

Vietnamese presents a useful and challenging setting for this research. Social-media writing commonly contains omitted diacritics, abbreviations, code-switching, expressive repetition, and context-dependent phrases. Whitespace alone does not consistently identify lexical word boundaries. A phrase such as "buồn ngủ" refers to sleepiness, whereas "buồn" in another context can describe sadness. Similarly, encouragement directed toward someone else can contain the same vocabulary as a first-person account of distress. A classifier that primarily associates isolated words with positive labels can therefore achieve high recall while generating many false positives.

Pretrained language models offer contextual representations that may help resolve such ambiguity. PhoBERT provides a Vietnamese-specific encoder and has demonstrated strong performance on several Vietnamese language-processing tasks [4]. However, an effective encoder cannot substitute for a valid target definition or a suitable evaluation set. Vietnamese sentiment and emotion resources provide useful text, but their labels describe related constructs rather than the particular depression-related language studied here. UIT-VSMEC, for example, is a social-media emotion corpus [5], not a set of clinically assessed individuals. Mapping its emotions into two classes creates an auxiliary transfer task whose limitations must remain explicit.

This study addresses the practical problem of constructing a Vietnamese comment-level benchmark under limited annotation resources. We collect YouTube comments, apply a transparent keyword-based scoring system, and use blind human annotation with iterative uncertainty-based selection. The resulting corpus supports comparisons between lexical, recurrent, contextual, and topic-based representations. Our contribution is primarily a dataset and evaluation workflow. The hybrid representation is examined as a complementary feature combination; the experiments do not establish a new state-of-the-art architecture or a diagnostic system.

Three research questions organize the study. First, can a high-recall weak labeler assist the construction of a human-labeled corpus without being treated as a source of definitive labels? Second, how do sparse lexical models, BiLSTM, PhoBERT, and topic features compare on the same in-domain benchmark? Third, what happens when the resulting classifiers are applied to an external emotion-derived task with a different class balance and annotation target? These questions link dataset design to model behavior rather than treating data preparation as a preliminary implementation detail.
The contributions are as follows:

• A Vietnamese YouTube data resource: 125,329 collected comments and a 9,134-example labeled benchmark, with a documented target definition, field schema, stage-specific statistics, and representative examples. • A data construction workflow combining weighted lexical retrieval, blind contextual annotation, and uncertainty-based selection. The weak labeler is assessed separately from the final classifiers. • A comparison of six classifier configurations on the constructed YouTube test and an existing UIT-VSMEC emotion-proxy test, with class-weighting ablation, confusion-matrix analysis, and contextual error analysis. These contributions concern a dataset and an empirical benchmark, rather than a new diagnostic model. The experiments test whether contextual representations improve on strong lexical baselines and whether their behavior persists under an external label mapping. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related research and Vietnamese resources. Section III describes VietDepression construction, explains each workflow stage, and presents dataset statistics and examples. Section IV reports model configurations, evaluation, comparative results, ablation, and limitations. Section V concludes the paper and identifies future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Research relevant to this task falls into social-media mental-health analysis, Vietnamese language resources, and methods that reduce annotation cost. Table 1 summarizes how these lines relate to the present benchmark.

div.head: A. SOCIAL MEDIA LANGUAGE AND MENTAL HEALTH
div.p: De Choudhury et al. investigated depression-related information in social-media activity [1], while Coppersmith et al. examined mental-health signals in Twitter language [2]. Yates et al. studied depression and selfharm risk in online forums [3]. These studies establish several relevant directions: language can contain useful signals, the data source affects the available evidence, and evaluation depends on how the target labels were obtained. Their results do not directly establish the performance of a Vietnamese comment-level classifier, because languages, platforms, annotation procedures, and units of analysis differ.

This distinction shapes the present task. User-level studies may aggregate many posts, whereas a commentlevel system receives a single text. Temporal persistence, personal history, and the relationship between comments are then unavailable. A phrase can be compatible with distress without providing enough evidence to infer a persistent condition. We therefore use depression-related language as an operational text label. Broader clinical concepts motivate the subject matter but are not converted into diagnostic claims about individual users.

Lexical features remain relevant in this setting because many explicit expressions are recognizable through words or short phrases. Their transparency also makes them useful for identifying failure cases and checking whether a more complex model offers meaningful gains. However, a high score on a lexically enriched dataset can partly reflect overlap between collection queries, annotation cues, and the features learned by the classifier. Including a strong lexical comparator is consequently necessary for interpreting the benefit of contextual modeling.

div.head: B. VIETNAMESE MODELS AND RELATED DATASETS
div.p: The Transformer architecture introduced attentionbased sequence modeling [6]. BERT demonstrated the value of bidirectional pretraining for downstream language understanding [7], and RoBERTa examined improvements to that training approach [8]. PhoBERT

In our experiments, its contextual representation serves both a fine-tuned classifier and the contextual branch of a hybrid model. Contextual encoding is relevant because the same Vietnamese term can appear in self-disclosure, figurative language, or supportive speech. The expected benefit is not simply better keyword recognition; it is improved use of surrounding information. Nevertheless, representations learned from pretraining and subsequent task adaptation can remain sensitive to source-specific language. We evaluate PhoBERT against a BiLSTM and sparse lexical models to separate the practical value of contextual pretraining from the assumption that a larger architecture will always perform better.

Vietnamese emotion and sentiment resources occupy a related but distinct position. UIT-VSMEC contains emotion-annotated social-media sentences [5], whereas UIT-VSFC concerns student feedback [9]. These resources should not be conflated. They can support auxiliary representation learning, negative-example construction, or transfer experiments, but their original labels do not directly establish the target label used in VietDepression. The mapping applied to an external resource is therefore part of the experimental definition rather than an inherent property of that resource.

div.head: C. WEAK SUPERVISION AND ACTIVE LEARNING
div.p: Weak labeling offers a way to prioritize an otherwise large unlabeled collection. In a rule-based system, candidate phrases contribute positive or negative evidence, and thresholds produce provisional classes or abstentions. The rules are inexpensive to apply and easy to inspect, but they encode only a partial account of meaning. A rule matching"mệt mỏi" can retrieve relevant material while also identifying routine physical fatigue. Weak labels are therefore most useful when their error profile is measured and their provenance remains distinct from human judgments.

Active learning selects examples for annotation using information from the current model. Settles describes the general framework and its alternatives [10]. Uncer-tainty sampling is attractive for binary classification because examples close to a decision boundary may reveal distinctions that the model has not learned. However, increased performance over successive rounds does not, by itself, establish annotation efficiency. A matched random-sampling comparison is needed to determine whether uncertainty-based selection yields more benefit for the same annotation budget.

Blind annotation addresses a different issue. Hiding machine labels and confidence values reduces an obvious source of anchoring during review. This interface design is compatible with active learning because examples can be selected using a model without showing its predictions to annotators. Agreement between the model and a human then measures correspondence between their decisions; it does not measure agreement between independent human annotators. This distinction is maintained throughout the present study.

div.head: D. TOPIC REPRESENTATIONS AND ADAPTATION
div.p: BERTopic combines document embeddings, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and class-based TF-IDF to produce interpretable topic descriptors [11]. Sentence-BERT provides a widely used approach to sentence representation [12], while UMAP and density-based clustering support the dimensionality reduction and grouping stages [13], [14]. In this study, topics provide information about the broad subject of a comment, potentially complementing its contextual representation.

Topical relevance and the target label are nevertheless different. A discussion of treatment may concern the writer, another person, or general advice. A musicrelated topic may contain both emotional self-disclosure and comments about the performance. We consequently evaluate topic-only classification separately from the hybrid representation. Topic names are used for corpus exploration, not as evidence that a classifier has identified a clinical state or a causal explanation for a prediction.

Domain-adaptive pretraining provides another way to use unlabeled text. Gururangan et al. show that additional pretraining on domain and task data can VOLUME 11, 2023 improve downstream models [15]. Such adaptation is relevant to informal Vietnamese, but it also raises an evaluation question: which documents were available during representation learning? Keeping external labels out of supervised training is insufficient to establish a strictly inductive test if the external texts were included in topic fitting or language-model adaptation. We return to this issue when defining the scope of the transfer results.

div.head: III. VIETDEPRESSION DATASET CONSTRUCTION A. ETHICS STATEMENT
div.p: This study used publicly available YouTube comments and did not involve direct interaction with or recruitment of human participants. No personally identifiable information was intentionally collected or reported.

div.head: B. DATA CONSTRUCTION WORKFLOW
div.p: The central resource of this study is a Vietnamese comment-level benchmark for depression-related language. This section follows the workflow in Figure 1: define the target, retrieve comments, normalize and filter text, prioritize candidates, obtain contextual human labels, and construct evaluation partitions. Each stage has a distinct input and output; provisional labels and external emotion labels are kept separate from the final in-domain annotation target.

div.head: C. TASK DEFINITION AND WORKFLOW OVERVIEW
div.p: Let x denote the normalized text of one comment and y ∈ {0, 1}. The positive class represents language annotated as expressing depression-related distress, while the negative class represents text not assigned that label. The classifier estimates a score p(y = 1 | x), or a decision function in the case of a linear support-vector classifier. The target is a text judgment under an annotation scheme. The negative class does not certify an absence of depression in the author, and the positive class does not certify its presence.

The annotation focus includes sadness, loss of motivation, hopelessness, isolation, and negative selfevaluation. These themes guide retrieval and review rather than acting as independently diagnosed symptoms. Their interpretation depends on context: a supportive reply can mention sadness without expressing the writer's own distress, and a brief statement of uncertainty can remain ambiguous. The corpus construction process allows uncertain and excluded examples during review rather than requiring every collected comment to receive a definitive binary label.

The unit of analysis also determines the scope of conclusions. This work does not predict severity, estimate onset, or link repeated comments to an individual trajectory. Video identifiers are retained for grouping, but author profiles and behavioral histories are not model inputs. Any relationship between comment-level classification and person-level assessment requires a separate study with an appropriate reference standard.
The workflow has six operational stages.

Step 1 records comments and source metadata. Step 2 produces normalized text and a filtered inventory. Step 3 applies weighted rules to prioritize review and retains uncertain cases. Step 4 presents text-only annotation tasks. Step 5 iterates model fitting and uncertain-example selection using training-eligible annotations. Step 6 defines the labeled benchmark and its train, validation, and test partitions. The evaluation block then compares models on the YouTube test and the external emotion-proxy task.

The diagram expresses the intended processing design, not proof that every stage count is linked by a complete lineage manifest. In particular, weak-label counts are recorded near the raw collection total, while the cleaned inventory has a different size. We therefore report both counts with their stage definitions and do not treat the weak-label inventory as a verified partition of the filtered pool.

div.head: D. STEP 1 DATA COLLECTION AND RECORD SCHEMA
div.p: YouTube was selected because public comments provide naturally occurring Vietnamese text associated with identifiable video contexts. Collection used the YouTube Data API v3 [16]. The search configuration targeted videos using Vietnamese relevance settings and the VN region code, ordered results by relevance, and requested up to 50 results per search page. The collection design allowed up to 100 videos per query and up to 100 toplevel comment threads per video. These bounds describe the collection procedure rather than a complete sample of YouTube activity.

The search vocabulary contained a reported total of 264 queries covering depression and suicidality, loneliness and sadness, stress and burnout, sleep disturbance and overthinking, and help-seeking or healing. These retrieval themes were designed to increase the proportion of relevant material in the pool. They should be distinguished from the 335 scoring entries used later for weak labeling. The retrieval vocabulary determines which discussions can enter the sample; the scoring vocabulary determines how their comments are provisionally categorized.

The collected schema comprised comment identifier, video identifier, video title, retrieval keyword, comment text, like count, and publication timestamp. Identifiers and source fields support deduplication and split auditing. They are not included as predictive features in the text classifiers. The availability of publication timestamps enables later temporal analysis, but no prospective temporal evaluation is established by the experiments reported here.

Ethical considerations. The collected data consist of publicly available YouTube comments written by identi- fiable individuals without their explicit informed consent for research use. Mental-health disclosures are inherently sensitive: their exposure may cause personal distress, social stigma, or reputational harm to the writers even when anonymized identifiers are removed. To mitigate re-identification risk, the public dataset release excludes verbatim comment text that can be directly searched on YouTube; only de-identified identifiers and annotation labels are shared. Researchers who obtain access to the full labeled corpus should apply the same principle: do not publish or share raw comment excerpts that allow a third party to locate the original poster's contributions without their consent.

The collection produced 125,329 comments. The processing inventory additionally records 119,649 comments after deduplication and filtering. We retain these as separate stages rather than describing both counts as the same cleaned corpus. Keyword-driven retrieval introduces selection bias toward discussions of distress and related themes; neither the weak-positive fraction nor the labeled-positive fraction estimates population prevalence. Table 2 summarizes these collected fields, distinguishes source and audit metadata from the text input, and records which fields are excluded from classification.

The schema makes source grouping explicit. Retaining video identifiers supports split assignment, while comment identifiers and normalized text address different duplication mechanisms. The classifier sees the comment text rather than a video title, search query, engagement count, or author profile. This separation matters because a retrieval keyword can reveal why a record was collected without providing evidence that the writer expresses personal distress. The five query themes broaden retrieval beyond the exact name of the condition: depression and suicidality; loneliness and sadness; stress and burnout; sleep disturbance and overthinking; and help-seeking or healing. Counts per theme are not reported as independent strata because a video or comment can be retrieved under more than one query. The 264 retrieval queries and 335 later scoring entries serve different purposes and are not interchangeable lexicons.

div.head: E. STEP 2 NORMALIZATION AND QUALITY FILTERING
div.p: Preprocessing was designed to preserve potentially meaningful linguistic information. Unicode NFC normalization and whitespace standardization were applied, while Vietnamese diacritics, emoji, and original case were retained. This choice avoids automatically removing emotional or orthographic cues before their relevance can be evaluated. The model-specific processing stage subsequently determines how the normalized text is segmented or encoded.

The filtering rules targeted promotional URLs, selected advertising phrases, extreme character repetition, and comments with very low lexical variety. A minimum length of five characters was imposed after normalization. Deduplication first used comment identifiers and then normalized text, retaining the first occurrence. The two checks address repeated API retrieval and repeated content, respectively. Exact text deduplication does not remove every paraphrase or shared quotation, so it cannot alone establish complete independence between splits.

Cleaning involves a trade-off. Repeated characters can be spam, but they can also express emphasis; links can advertise a service, but they can also accompany helpseeking or support. The resulting benchmark is therefore conditional on the filtering rules. Future dataset revisions should retain exclusion reasons and inspect samples near rule boundaries, allowing researchers to assess whether cleaning disproportionately removes particular forms of distress-related expression.

The difference between the raw and filtered inventories is 5,680 records, or approximately 4.53% of the 125,329 collected comments. This is an aggregate reduction; the available inventory does not allocate it among duplicates, advertising, short texts, or other filters. Thus, it cannot support claims about the percentage removed by an individual rule. Likewise, text-length means, standard deviations, and vocabulary coverage require the underlying row-level corpus and are not inferred from collection totals.

The preserved and transformed information follows the text-classification objective. Diacritics distinguish Vietnamese words; negation and speaker perspective affect whether an expression concerns the author or another person. Cleaning should therefore standardize representation without turning context-dependent phrases into isolated keywords. Model-specific word segmentation is applied later, so corpus normalization is not conflated with a particular model tokenizer.

div.head: F. STEP 3 WEIGHTED LABELING AND CANDIDATE SELECTION
div.p: The weak labeler uses three sets of scoring entries: 53 strong positive indicators, 116 context-dependent positive indicators, and 166 normal-context indicators. The total of 335 refers to these scoring entries. A further set of 22 review-context phrases flags cases that require contextual inspection; it is not added to the scoring total. Table 3 summarizes the groups and their intended roles.
For a comment x, let n s (x), n m (x), and n n (x) denote the matches in the strong, medium, and normal-context groups. The score is defined as

The system assigns a provisional positive label when s(x) ≥ 5, a provisional negative label when s(x) ≤ -2, and an uncertain status when -1 ≤ s(x) ≤ 4. Positive labels are considered high-confidence when s(x) ≥ 8, while negative labels are considered high-confidence when s(x) ≤ -4. The thresholds encode a practical retrieval policy. They do not represent calibrated probabilities or clinical severity levels.

The subtraction of normal-context evidence helps reduce some obvious false positives, but additive scoring cannot fully model compositional meaning. For example, a supportive sentence can contain several positive indicators while remaining directed toward another person. Conversely, an implicit expression may receive a low score despite being judged relevant by a human. The uncertain category is therefore central to the pipeline: it prevents an absence of strong lexical evidence from being treated automatically as a reliable negative label.

The weak-label distribution records 3,223 provisional positives, 23,695 provisional negatives, and 98,410 uncertain examples. The counts total 125,328, one below the collected inventory. We preserve the category counts without assigning the residual record to a class. Approximately 78.52% of the scored inventory is uncertain, indicating that the rules provide confident coverage for only a minority of the collection. A separate review flag occurs on 120,334 records and overlaps the provisional classes; it is not a fourth mutually exclusive class.

The weak label has a procedural role: it determines which comments are easy to retrieve and which need contextual review. An uncertain comment is not an automatic negative example. Similarly, a review-context flag is metadata about a possible linguistic ambiguity, not a fourth class that can be added to positive, negative, and uncertain totals. This distinction prevents the same record from being counted more than once in classdistribution summaries.

div.head: G. STEPS 4 AND 5 BLIND ANNOTATION AND ACTIVE LEARNING
div.p: Annotation was conducted through Label Studio. The review interface displayed comment text and a row identifier while excluding machine labels, scores, and confidence values. This separation allows model-based selection of examples without presenting the model's proposed answer to the annotator. Uncertain and excluded judgments were retained during review, and the final benchmark contains binary labels after the datasetconstruction process.

The active-learning workflow alternates model fitting, scoring of an unlabeled pool, selection of uncertain examples, blind review, and incorporation of newly labeled data. For a binary model with probability p(x), a least- confidence score can be expressed as

Larger values correspond to predictions closer to 0.5. Equation ( 2) describes the uncertainty principle used by the workflow; the records do not provide a complete perround selection manifest or a fixed batch size covering every stage. Six rounds were completed, with stopping linked to performance and annotation budget. Figure 1 places this iteration between candidate scoring and final benchmark construction.

Two documented batches provide information about human-machine correspondence. Batch 5 contains 750 reviewed samples, a disagreement rate of 17.49%, and Cohen's κ of 0.63. Batch 8 contains 1,000 samples, a disagreement rate of 53.72%, and κ of -0.03. These are human-machine agreement statistics. They cannot be used as estimates of inter-annotator reliability, because the comparison is not between two independently labeling humans.

The lower agreement on the active-learning batch is compatible with the selection of difficult cases, but it does not prove that the interface eliminated bias or that the human labels are correct. The batch identifiers also should not be equated with the six active-learning rounds: annotation batches and training rounds represent different organizational units. A complete reliability analysis would require overlapping human annotations, a defined adjudication procedure, and agreement estimates calculated on that overlap.

Representative decisions should be interpreted at the comment level. First-person exhaustion and reduced motivation can receive the positive text label. Encouragement addressed to someone else and the expression "buồn ngủ" can receive the negative label even when a lexical rule detects a distress-related term. Ambiguous cases require contextual judgment rather than a diagnosis inferred from a single word. Table 7 later illustrates these distinctions using examples already recorded in the source study.

The two documented review batches contain 1,750 reviewed records in total, whereas the final labeled inventory contains 9,134. They do not by themselves reconstruct the provenance of every final label. A complete release should connect row identifiers to review history and retain unresolved or excluded decisions. The present article therefore distinguishes the reported final inventory from the smaller batches for which review statistics are available.

div.head: H. ANNOTATION QUALITY AND WEAK-LABEL VALIDATION
div.p: The weak labeler was evaluated on 343 examples with human labels and evaluable binary predictions. The recorded confusion counts are 92 true positives, 191 true negatives, 58 false positives, and two false negatives. These counts yield positive-class precision of 0.6133, recall of 0.9787, accuracy of 0.8251, and macro F1 of 0.8092. Table 4 reports the metrics together with the denominator so that the high recall is not mistaken for performance on the full collection.

The asymmetry between precision and recall is consistent with a retrieval-oriented rule set. Only two positive examples were missed within this evaluable subset, but 58 negative examples were flagged as positive. The resulting positive-class F1 is 0.7541, which differs from macro F1 because the latter averages the scores of both classes. In practice, the rules can reduce the effort required to locate candidate material, while a contextual review step remains necessary to distinguish personal distress from other uses of the same phrases.

These estimates also depend on how the 343 examples were selected and how uncertain outputs were handled. They do not quantify recall over every implicit expression in the unlabeled pool. A complete validation should include both confident and abstained examples sampled under a documented design. The current results support weak labeling as an annotation aid, rather than as an automatic replacement for human labels.

Human-machine agreement and weak-label validation answer different questions. The former measures correspondence on selected annotation batches; the latter measures the rule system against reference labels in an evaluable subset. Neither is a substitute for independent inter-annotator agreement across the final benchmark. The high weak-label recall should therefore be read as evidence for candidate retrieval, while annotation consistency remains a separate quality dimension.

div.head: I. STEP 6 BENCHMARK PARTITIONING AND DATASET STATISTICS
div.p: The final labeled benchmark contains The split design combines class stratification with video-level separation, so comments associated with the same video are intended to remain within one partition. The rationale is to reduce shared contextual information across training and evaluation. External resources are assigned separate roles, and keyword distributions are considered during partitioning. These design choices reduce obvious leakage risks, but a claim of verified independence requires the actual identifiers, text hashes, and assignment files.

There is an additional distinction between supervised separation and representation-learning separation. A model trained on topic features can have indirect access to evaluation text if the topic model was fitted on the complete corpus. The same issue applies to domainadaptive pretraining. The corpus inventory does not establish a strict exclusion list for these stages. Accordingly, the topic and adaptation results are treated as exploratory, and the external experiment is not presented as a fully audited inductive benchmark.

The final labeled inventory represents approximately 7.29% of the raw collection, and its positive share is 19.75%. This fraction describes a selected, annotated benchmark rather than a population sample. The YouTube test has nearly the same positive share, 19.77%, with about 4.06 negative comments per positive comment. These statistics motivate class-balanced losses and macro-averaged evaluation rather than accuracy alone.

By contrast, the external test is balanced at 50% positive proxies. This is a deliberate experimental composition, not evidence that half of the source population expresses depression-related language. Figure 2 makes the distinction between provisional weak-label coverage, benchmark class balance, and external proxy composition visible. Uncertain weak outputs are not included in the binary test metrics.

Train and validation class totals should not be obtained by independently rounding a 70/15/15 split of the positive class. Grouping by video can affect exact assignments, and a reproducible split requires the actual manifest. The stated partition sizes are retained as reported, while exact class supports are given only where the numerical records supply them. The first two positive examples combine first-person perspective with exhaustion, loss of motivation, or recurring isolation. The implicit example expresses stagnation without naming depression; its reported label depends on the annotation context. In contrast, the supportive example directs reassurance to another person. A bag of isolated distress words can miss this change in perspective.

The sleepiness example demonstrates a lexical ambiguity specific to phrase composition: "buồn ngủ" does not mean the same thing as sadness in isolation. The deadline example shows why tiredness should not automatically determine the positive class. These distinctions justify both a contextual encoder and a strong lexical baseline: the comparison asks whether contextual modeling improves on easily learned word associations.

The two UIT-VSMEC examples show why target mapping must be declared. The positive proxy is derived from an emotion label; no clinical assessment is implied. Good or poor performance on these examples can reflect agreement with the emotion mapping as well as crosssource language behavior. For reproducible qualitative analysis, future releases should retain example provenance privately and provide de-identified identifiers for the released subset.

div.head: K. EXTERNAL RESOURCES AND DATASET AVAILABILITY
div.p: Eight external Vietnamese resources contributed 191,072 texts to the wider corpus inventory. They include emotion, sentiment, and toxicity data with different annotation schemes. The recorded unified corpus contains 316,401 documents, equal to the collected YouTube count plus the external inventory. It is used for exploratory topic modeling and described as a source for language-model adaptation. Because this accounting is based on the collected count, it should not be interpreted as the size of a separately verified, fully deduplicated modeling pool. External data have three conceptually different roles. UIT-VSMEC supplies an emotion-derived transfer evaluation. Positive-affect examples from other resources form a candidate hard-negative pool of 42,952 texts. The remaining material contributes text for corpuslevel representation learning. These roles must remain distinguishable because supervised labels, pseudo-labels, and unlabeled exposure have different implications for model evaluation.

The construction record also describes a weighted training expansion with human labels, high-confidence rule labels, model pseudo-labels, and external negative examples. Those records are not interchangeable with the final 6,392-example benchmark training partition. Without a model-specific manifest, the final comparison cannot establish the independent effect of each expanded source. We therefore report the stable benchmark split explicitly and discuss the augmentation inventory as a separate component of the overall workflow.

Table 8 separates eight auxiliary resources by original task and recorded use. Only UIT-VSMEC contributes the reported external evaluation. Other sentiment and toxicity resources are described because they influence the wider corpus and candidate pools, not because independent depression-detection results were measured on each one. Their original labels cannot be silently relabeled as clinical ground truth.

The project repository is identified as https://github. com/iannwendy/aitraining. The recorded canonical dataset path is data/labeled/final_dataset.csv; auxiliary augmentation material is recorded under data/augmented_v2. A reproducible release needs versioned split assignments, annotation provenance, preprocessing rules, and model-specific fitting inventories. Public comment availability does not remove reidentification risk, so sharing decisions should account for source identifiers and searchable verbatim excerpts.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: The experiments evaluate six classifier configurations on two test resources: the newly constructed YouTube benchmark and an existing UIT-VSMEC subset mapped to an emotion-proxy task. The comparison covers lexical, recurrent, contextual, topic-only, and hybrid representations. We first define the evaluation sets and model settings, then examine overall scores, error structure, class weighting, and annotation-round progress.

div.head: A. EVALUATION DATASETS AND METRICS
div.p: The primary test contains UIT-VSMEC is a social-media emotion resource [5]. The transfer experiment changes dataset and label meaning simultaneously. Even a model that perfectly captures the original comment-level annotation policy may disagree with a mapping that treats every sadness or fear example as positive. Conversely, good performance on the proxy mapping would not validate depression detection. The construction of the balanced subset, including sampling, deduplication, and original split membership, requires a retained selection manifest for exact reproduction.

div.head: B. MODEL CONFIGURATIONS
div.p: The following configurations use text as input and differ in representation and classifier. They are practical benchmark systems; their comparison does not isolate every architectural factor.

div.head: 1) TF-IDF with linear classifiers
div.p: The lexical representation combines word-level TF-IDF unigrams and bigrams with character-level n-grams of length three to five. Each branch allows up to 80,000 features. Character features are restricted to within-word boundary patterns and are intended to capture spelling variation, including omitted diacritics and informal character sequences. Concatenating the two branches combines short lexical phrases with subword evidence without requiring pretrained contextual embeddings. Two linear classifiers are evaluated on sparse representations. LinearSVC uses balanced class weights and a maximum of 2,000 optimization iterations. Logistic regression provides an additional lexical comparator and is also evaluated with class weighting. The support-vector classifier supplies a margin-based decision, whereas logistic regression produces a probabilistic score through its link function. Their inclusion tests whether the principal distinctions in the benchmark can be learned from recurring lexical patterns.

The TF-IDF vocabulary and document-frequency statistics belong to the fitted model and should be estimated from training data. Applying the fitted transformation to validation and test data then preserves the separation between feature fitting and evaluation. Exact regularization settings for the logistic-regression comparator are not available in the numerical configuration summary, so its score is reported as a benchmark result without claiming a complete reproduction from the manuscript alone.

div.head: 2) Bidirectional LSTM
div.p: The BiLSTM uses a vocabulary of 15,000 tokens and a trainable 128-dimensional embedding layer. Two bidirectional layers use 128 hidden units per direction, yielding a 256-dimensional representation. Dropout of 0.5 is applied between recurrent layers. The classification head maps the representation through a 64-unit ReLU layer to two logits. This architecture provides a sequential baseline whose embeddings are learned within the task rather than supplied by a large pretrained language model.

The recorded training configuration uses Adam with learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, eight epochs, and a maximum sequence length of 100 tokens. The main configuration describes an unweighted loss, whereas the class-weighting comparison also reports a weighted BiLSTM result. Because the aggregate benchmark does not unambiguously identify which variant generated its score, we retain the reported aggregate result and treat the weighting comparison as a separate experimental record.

This distinction matters when interpreting a lower score. The comparison does not isolate recurrence from all other factors: pretraining, loss weighting, tokenization, maximum length, and optimization budget also differ. The experiment addresses which implemented configuration performs best on the benchmark, rather than establishing an architecture-only causal explanation.

div.head: 3) PhoBERT
div.p: PhoBERT-base is fine-tuned for binary classification
A corresponding weighted cross-entropy objective for a minibatch B is
div.formula: L = -(1/|B|) ∑︂ i∈B w yi log p(y i | x i )(6)
div.p: The recorded optimizer is AdamW with learning rate 2 × 10 -5 and weight decay 0.01. Training uses a batch size of eight, an evaluation batch size of 16, a maximum length of 128 tokens, gradient clipping at 1.0, and a linear warmup ratio of 0.06. The configuration allows three epochs with early-stopping patience of two. Model selection uses validation data, while the test partition serves final evaluation.

The PhoBERT benchmark records three seeds, 42, 123, and 2024. Its aggregate output is described using both voting and averaging terminology. Averaging scores over runs, averaging predicted probabilities, and majority voting are different operations; they can produce different confusion matrices and F1 values. We therefore identify the main score as the reported aggregate PhoBERT result and analyze the recorded confusion matrix separately. No standard deviation or significance claim is inferred from the existence of three seeds alone.

div.head: 4) Topic-only classification
div.p: The topic pipeline uses multilingual MiniLM sentence embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, and HDBSCAN clustering, followed by class-based TF-IDF descriptors [11], [12], [13], [14]. The fitted corpus inventory contains 316,401 texts. The recorded model discovers 456 topics and assigns 48.30% of documents to the outlier category. This substantial outlier fraction is relevant to classification because topic membership is unavailable or weak for a large portion of the corpus.

The topic-only classifier uses the assigned topic identifier and its probability as features for logistic regression. A topic identifier is categorical, not an ordered numerical quantity: adjacent identifiers do not imply similar topics. The available configuration does not fully specify the encoding or handling of outliers for this baseline. Its results should consequently be understood as an exploratory check of topical features rather than a complete test of every topic-based representation.

Topical descriptions provide a useful way to inspect the collection. They can reveal whether retrieval concentrated on treatment, sleep, work stress, music, or loneliness. However, an interpretable cluster label does not establish that every member expresses the positive target. Topic-only classification is expected to lose distinctions involving speaker perspective, negation, and implicit meaning that are expressed within otherwise similar subject matter.

div.head: 5) PhoBERT and BERTopic hybrid
div.p: The hybrid model concatenates a 768-dimensional PhoBERT representation h(x), a 456-dimensional onehot topic vector, and one topic-assignment probability. Its feature vector is

Here t(x) is the assigned topic and q(x) is the assignment probability. StandardScaler normalizes the concatenated features before a logistic-regression classifier with balanced class weights estimates the binary outcome. The stated dimension describes the discovered non-outlier topics; the outlier encoding must be specified in an executable release. Figure 3 shows the feature combination without assuming that cluster membership explains the model's decision. The underlying hypothesis is that contextual and topical information capture complementary aspects of the text. PhoBERT represents local and sentence-level meaning, while topic membership represents a broad thematic position within the corpus. The hybrid changes more than feature dimensionality: it also uses a logisticregression head rather than the end-to-end classification head of the fine-tuned PhoBERT model. Therefore, a comparison between the two does not isolate the effect of adding topics unless the remaining components are controlled.

The source record does not specify all details of checkpoint selection, encoder freezing, or feature-fitting partitions for the hybrid. Its in-domain score is nonetheless useful as a descriptive result. The comparison can establish whether the implemented combination exceeded the reported PhoBERT aggregate, but cannot establish a general benefit or disadvantage of topic augmentation across other fitting protocols.

div.head: C. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND REPRODUCIBILITY
div.p: Table 9 summarizes the main settings. The implementation uses a CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU with PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers [17], together with scikit-learn [18], underthesea, BERTopic, and sentencetransformers. The environment inventory gives lowerbound library versions rather than a fully pinned soft-ware environment and does not identify an exact GPU model. Consequently, computational cost and hardwarenormalized efficiency cannot be compared from the present records.

The recurrent and contextual models differ in training duration, input length, and pretraining. Classical classifiers use a single recorded seed, while PhoBERT and BiLSTM have aggregate results associated with multiple seeds. These are comparisons of practical configurations, not equal-compute experiments. Neither inference-time superiority nor lower variance is claimed without corresponding measurements. The same restraint applies to small differences in macro F1: they describe the reported scores but do not establish statistical significance.

div.head: D. COMPARATIVE RESULTS ON BOTH EVALUATION SETS
div.p: Table 10 presents the available macro-F1 results. The six rows include two lexical classifiers and one classifier for each of the recurrent, contextual, topic-only, and hybrid settings. This distinction resolves the difference between five representation families and six evaluated classifier configurations. For the hybrid external result, the dedicated topic-results record distinguishes accuracy of 0.5084 from macro F1 of 0.3674; the latter is used here.

PhoBERT has the highest reported in-domain macro F1, 0.7187. The hybrid follows at 0.7153, and TF-IDF with logistic regression obtains 0.7138. The differences from PhoBERT are only 0.0034 and 0.0049, respectively, equivalent to 0.34 and 0.49 percentage points. Lin-earSVC scores 0.7025, BiLSTM 0.6418, and the topiconly classifier 0.4208. These results show that the contextual model is competitive, while also demonstrating that a sparse lexical baseline captures much of the available in-domain signal.

The hybrid does not improve the reported in-domain score over PhoBERT. One possible explanation is redundancy between thematic information and the contextual representation; another is that coarse topics do not encode the distinction between personal distress and discussion of distress. The current experiment does not isolate these mechanisms. The result supports retaining topic modeling for corpus interpretation, but does not support claiming that topic concatenation improves the classifier.

On the external proxy task, BERTopic-only obtains 0.5030 and BiLSTM 0.3375. LinearSVC scores 0.3798, the hybrid 0.3674, PhoBERT 0.3608, and TF-IDF with logistic regression 0.3577. Thus, topic-only classification achieves the highest external score, notably outperforming all fine-tuned models. TF-IDF + LinearSVC follows at 0.3798, while BiLSTM records the lowest external F1 at 0.3375, below PhoBERT and its hybrid variant. Figure 4 displays the complete comparison.

The external results warrant stronger language than 'generalization gap.' A trivial baseline that always predicts the majority class on a balanced test set achieves Scores near 0.50 macro F1 on a balanced task indicate limited discrimination and should not be described as successful transfer without further context. For reference, always predicting one class on a balanced binary set gives macro F1 of one third; independent, equally likely random predictions have an expected large-sample macro F1 near one half. These analytical reference points are not measured additional baselines. They clarify why outperforming a collapsed one-class predictor is insufficient evidence of robust generalization.

The reported transfer gap is 0.3579 for PhoBERT, 0.3561 for TF-IDF with logistic regression, 0.3479 for the hybrid, 0.3227 for LinearSVC, and 0.3043 for BiLSTM. BERTopic-only has a negative gap of -0.0822 because its external score exceeds its in-domain score. A smaller gap is not automatically preferable: a weak model can perform poorly in both settings. Absolute scores and the meaning of each label set must be considered alongside the difference.

div.head: E. CONFUSION MATRICES AND CLASS-SPECIFIC BEHAVIOR
div.p: The recorded PhoBERT confusion matrices reveal a marked change in positive predictions. In-domain, 182 of 271 positive comments are correctly identified, while 89 are missed. Among 1,100 negative comments, 194 are incorrectly flagged and 906 are correctly classified. In the Figure 5 shows the counts using rows for reference labels and columns for predictions. Metrics calculated directly from these counts are listed in Table 11. In-domain positive precision is 0.4840 and recall is 0.6716; external positive precision is 0.8167 and recall is only 0.0318. The higher external precision reflects a very small set of positive predictions: just 60 of 3,084 examples, or 1.95%. It should not obscure the failure to retrieve most positive proxy examples. The matrix therefore supports a specific conclusion of negative-class prediction collapse under the external mapping.

The matrix-derived macro F1 values are 0.7138 indomain and 0.3659 externally, rather than the aggregate values 0.7187 and 0.3608 in Table 10. Similarly, the in-domain matrix yields accuracy 0.7936. We do not combine these statistics into a single purported run. Different checkpoints, seeds, or aggregation procedures could produce distinct outputs, but the present records do not identify which explanation applies. The macro- F1 comparison and the count-based error analysis consequently remain separate evidence streams.

The in-domain negative-only accuracy reference is 1,100/1,371 = 0.8023, but its macro F1 is only 0.4452. This demonstrates why accuracy alone is inadequate. The recorded classifier matrix has slightly lower accuracy than the negative-only rule while achieving substantially higher macro F1 through nonzero positive recall. Model selection should therefore reflect the desired error trade-off rather than a single overall correctness percentage.

div.head: F. ABLATION AND ACTIVE-LEARNING DEVELOPMENT
div.p: Table 12 summarizes the recorded class-weighting comparison. PhoBERT increases from 0.6523 without weighting to 0.7187 with weighting, a gain of 0.0664. TF-IDF with logistic regression increases from 0.5891 to 0.7138, a gain of 0.1247. BiLSTM increases from 0.6312 to 0.6418, a gain of 0.0106. The observed range is therefore 1.09 to 12.47 macro-F1 percentage points, rather than a range that excludes the smaller recurrentmodel gain.

These results are consistent with class weighting being useful under the benchmark imbalance, especially for logistic regression. They do not establish that weighting is optimal for every deployment distribution or that all improvements arise from the same error changes. 11.

Per-class confusion matrices for the ablation variants would be needed to determine whether gains reflect better positive recall, fewer false positives, or both. The BiLSTM configuration ambiguity described earlier also limits direct correspondence between its ablation and aggregate rows.

The active-learning record shows in-domain macro F1 of 0.5821, 0.6314, 0.6658, 0.6892, 0.7015, and 0.7187 across six rounds. The overall increase is 0.1366. Gains between consecutive rounds are 0.0493, 0.0344, 0.0234, 0.0123, and 0.0172. Progress generally slows after the early rounds, but the final increment is larger than the preceding increment, so the trajectory is not strictly diminishing.

The sample counts associated with early rounds are approximate, and the final round incorporates the much larger 9,134-example benchmark. Consequently, the curve is evidence of development progress rather than a controlled label-efficiency experiment. It does not establish how many annotations active learning saved compared with random sampling. Such a claim would require equal budgets, identical model configurations, and a fixed evaluation set across sampling strategies.

The left panel in Figure 6 isolates the recorded withweight versus without-weight comparisons, subject to the BiLSTM correspondence issue. The right panel records development across six rounds. These panels address different questions: a loss-weight comparison and an annotation-driven training trajectory. They should not be combined into a claim that active learning itself caused the entire observed improvement.

div.head: G. QUALITATIVE ERRORS AND CORPUS TOPICS
div.p: Qualitative examples reveal three recurring ambiguities. First, a comment such as "đừng buồn nữa nhé" is directed toward another person and may be supportive, despite containing a sadness term. Second, "buồn ngủ" denotes sleepiness and illustrates how phrase-level meaning can differ from the isolated word "buồn." Third, expressions such as "mình chẳng biết phải làm sao nữa" can communicate helplessness without explicitly naming a condition. The last example is also intrinsically underspecified: interpretation depends on context and should not be treated as a universal diagnostic cue.

These examples motivate contextual modeling, but they do not prove that PhoBERT always resolves the ambiguity. The recorded in-domain false positives and false negatives show that substantial errors remain. A few selected examples can illustrate mechanisms, whereas their frequency in the population requires a systematic sample with consistent coding. We therefore use the examples as an error taxonomy and avoid converting them into unsupported rates of success on implicit language.

The topic model identifies clusters associated with treatment, sleep, workplace stress, sadness, and loneliness. The recorded counts include 749 documents in the treatment-related topic, 1,687 in the sleep-related topic, 1,052 in the work-stress topic, 1,214 in the sadnessrelated topic, and 844 in the loneliness-related topic. These are cluster sizes within the broader corpus, not counts of clinically depressed users or verified positive examples.

The 48.30% outlier rate further limits reliance on topics as complete semantic coverage. Topic features may be useful for selecting material for review and understanding retrieval bias, yet their low in-domain macro F1 of 0.4208 shows that broad subject matter alone is insufficient in the evaluated implementation. The hybrid result suggests that simply appending topic membership does not resolve the distinction between talking about distress and expressing it.

div.head: H. INTERPRETATION AND LIMITATIONS
div.p: The external experiment exposes an important weakness: predictions that identify many positive YouTube examples become predominantly negative under the emotion-derived evaluation. This is evidence that the trained decision policy does not align well with the external proxy labels. It is not, by itself, evidence that a formal writing style causes the failure, since UIT-VSMEC is a social-media corpus and the study does not measure register differences in a controlled way.

At least three changes occur together. The source collection and its selection process differ; the positive label changes from contextual distress annotation to sadnessor-fear membership; and the class balance changes from about one fifth positive to one half positive. Any or all of these can affect the observed metrics. Their individual contributions cannot be identified from one comparison. Describing the gap as entirely a model-generalization failure would therefore overstate what the design isolates.

The small in-domain margins do not establish statistical significance. Confidence intervals, paired prediction files, and complete per-seed outputs are needed to compare models statistically. Likewise, computational efficiency cannot be inferred without a pinned environment and hardware measurements. The main result is a descriptive benchmark ranking, not proof of architectural superiority under equal computational budgets.

Annotation quality and sampling constrain the dataset contribution. Keyword retrieval favors particular discussions, the final label ledger is only partly documented, and reported human-machine agreement is not inter-annotator reliability. The positive fractions therefore characterize the constructed samples rather than prevalence in the Vietnamese population. Exactduplicate filtering and video-grouped split intentions are useful controls, but a leakage audit requires identifiers, text hashes, and representation-fitting manifests.

The topic model and adaptation corpus may contain evaluation texts even when external labels are excluded from supervised training. The external experiment is therefore not presented as a fully audited inductive benchmark. Domain-adaptive pretraining and augmentation summaries are not used as central quantitative evidence because their baseline alignment and uncertainty are insufficiently documented.

Finally, this classifier concerns language in individual comments. It has not been validated for clinical diagnosis, crisis intervention, or person-level risk assessment. Its supported uses are methodological comparison, aggregate error analysis, and further annotation research. The distinction between distress-related text and an author's clinical state remains essential to interpreting every result.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: This study introduced VietDepression, establishing a data construction and benchmarking framework for detecting depression-related language in Vietnamese YouTube comments. We demonstrated that combining a weighted weak-labeling lexicon with active learning effectively filters and prioritizes large-scale social media text for manual review. Our empirical comparisons show that Vietnamese pre-trained language models like PhoBERT serve as effective contextual baselines for indomain distress detection, significantly outperforming recurrence-based approaches while remaining competitive with feature-rich lexical models.

Despite these achievements, several limitations re-main. Cross-domain transfer evaluation revealed significant drops in performance due to domain shifts, differences in annotation targets, and varying class distributions. Furthermore, simple topic concatenation failed to resolve complex linguistic ambiguities such as supportive speech, implicit expressions, or polysemous terms. Future work will focus on improving annotation quality through independent inter-annotator agreement studies, releasing versioned split manifests, and strictly excluding held-out text from representation pretraining. We also plan to evaluate models across diverse multi-platform sources using aligned depression-related guidelines to isolate domain shift from target label mismatch.

The next experimental step is a matched annotationbudget comparison between uncertainty sampling and random selection, using a fixed evaluation set. Crosssource evaluation should then use multiple platforms annotated under the same depression-related language rubric. This would separate source changes from emotion-to-distress label mismatch. Targeted analysis of negation, supportive speech, polysemy, and implicit expression would test whether contextual models improve the distinctions that matter for this task.

VietDepression provides a foundation for Vietnamese comment-level research through its data construction workflow and multi-model comparison. Its current evidence favors PhoBERT slightly in-domain, while emphasizing that better annotation documentation and aligned external labels are necessary for stronger claims of generalization.
